profile.summary: ESCOTT predicts how damaging each possible amino acid substitution in a protein would be. It is not a trained network: it scores mutations from a multiple sequence alignment the user supplies, using the evolutionary distances between natural sequences to capture epistasis and conservation, together with a model structure such as one from AlphaFold. The output is a complete matrix of predicted effects for the protein. ESCOTT is one of two programs in the PRESCOTT package; the other, PRESCOTT, adjusts these scores with population allele frequencies from gnomAD for clinical classification.

summary_quotes.text: to introduce ESCOTT, an epistatic and structural model of mutational effects
Leveraging protein sequences, structural models, and population-specific allele frequencies, PRESCOTT surpasses existing methods in classifying ClinVar variants
It is made up of two main programs: escott and prescott.
ESCOTT can calculate effects of single point mutations and multiple point mutations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESCOTT scores a missense mutation from two sources of information. The first is evolutionary: the distances between natural sequences in a multiple sequence alignment, which carry both epistatic information and the conservation of each position, following the GEMME approach. The second is structural: a model structure, in practice from AlphaFold. The score combines an epistatic term and an independent term, with a linear coefficient set to 0.6 by default in favour of the epistatic term. Without a structure file the program still produces a full mutational matrix, which the paper says then corresponds to iGEMME, their improved version of GEMME. ESCOTT is the part of the PRESCOTT package that does not use allele frequencies; PRESCOTT then adjusts ESCOTT scores using gnomAD population frequencies.

sections.title: What it needs and what it gives back
sections.body: ESCOTT takes a multiple sequence alignment in FASTA format, with the query protein as the first sequence and no gaps in it, and optionally but preferably a structure in PDB format. By default it predicts the effect of every possible single substitution at every position; a mutations file can restrict that, and multiple substitutions can be combined on one line. The developers warn that an alignment from ColabFold may contain gaps in the query sequence that have to be removed first, and that each alignment needs enough sequences.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ESCOTT is distributed as part of the PRESCOTT package rather than as a model checkpoint. The paper's software citation gives PRESCOTT source code version v1.6.0 under GPLv3, including iGEMME and ESCOTT, with a Zenodo deposit at 10.5281/zenodo.10442848 and a Docker image on Docker Hub. The repository read here is the LCQB GitLab project, pinned at commit 46fecb55 of the master branch, whose own commit date is 8 June 2025. A result should name the package version or commit, and the alignment and structure used, since both are user supplied and change the score.

sections.title: How this record was benchmarked
sections.body: The record comes from ProteinGym, whose README lists ESCOTT among the substitution benchmark baselines with multiple sequence alignment and structure as its input modalities, cites the preprint of this work, and names the LCQB GitLab project as the repository its code came from. ProteinGym's release notes record ESCOTT as one of the baselines added in version 1.2 of the benchmark. The paper reports the whole ProteinGym dataset of about 1.5 million mutations completing in 6.16 hours.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Alignment and structure based missense effect predictor, not a trained neural network; it is one of the two programs in the PRESCOTT package.

quotes.text: ESCOTT, an epistatic and structural model of mutational effects
PRESCOTT is a package predicting mutational effects in a protein based on population, evolutionary and structural information.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: A scoring model built on the GEMME approach: an epistatic term and an independent term combined by a linear coefficient, 0.6 by default towards the epistatic term, with structural terms from circular variance and physico-chemical properties when a structure is given.

quotes.text: This model is based on the GEMME approach
it uses the two-component max value terms, respectively combining circular variance, CV, and physico-chemical properties, PC, with evolutionary conservation
giving more weight to the epistatic contribution of the model

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A multiple sequence alignment in FASTA format with the query as the first, gap free sequence (mandatory), and a PDB structure file (optional but recommended). Optionally a file of single or multiple substitutions to score.
facts.source_locator: README: Input Data Requirements for escott; Running the escott program

quotes.text: escott requires two files:
a structure file in PDB format (optional but highly recommended)
a set of single or multiple mutations can be given with the option -m

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: A complete matrix of predicted effects for the query protein, written to text files; the file ending normPredCombi.txt is the one the prescott program then takes as input.
facts.source_locator: README: Input Data Requirements for prescott; paper: Methods

quotes.text: output file of escott (the file ending with ...normPredCombi.txt)
complete matrices describing mutational effects are provided

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: No trained parameter count: it is an alignment and structure based model, not a learned network. The sources give a default linear coefficient of 0.6 between its two terms, and say PRESCOTT's own thresholds were computed on a few hundred proteins.

quotes.text: is a linear coefficient set to 0.6 by default
PRESCOTT relies on a few parameters whose thresholds are computed on a small set of a few hundred proteins.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: None in the usual sense: the paper states that no training on human clinical data over large quantities of rare pathogenic and rare benign variants was done, and that ESCOTT relies solely on sequence and structure information. Each prediction uses the user's own alignment and structure.

quotes.text: No training on human clinical data over large quantities of rare pathogenic and rare benign variants is realized.
ESCOTT relies solely on sequence and structure information

facts.value: Not applicable: there is no trained model and no training corpus with a date. The inputs are the user's alignment and structure, and PRESCOTT's frequency step uses gnomAD, whose version the user supplies.

run_guide.summary: Get the package from the pinned commit of its GitLab repository, install it by the docs folder steps or use the Docker image, and score every single substitution in one protein with escott.
prerequisites: Linux: the README says the package has been tested only on Linux.
Python 3.9 or newer, as setup.py requires, plus R, which the README names as a second language of the implementation.
The dependencies in requirements.txt: prody, numpy below 1.24, matplotlib, scipy, pandas, biopython up to 1.79, biotite and scikit-learn.
A multiple sequence alignment for the query protein in FASTA format, query first and gap free, and preferably a PDB structure.
The developers recommend their Docker image or web site instead of a source install, because of the dependencies.

steps.explanation: The README's basic command, where inputAli.fasta is the alignment and input.pdb the structure. By default it scores all possible single mutations at all positions. Example input files for the BLAT protein are in the repository's data folder.

steps.title: Optionally add population frequencies
steps.explanation: The README's prescott example, run on its own bundled MLH1 files. It takes the escott output, a gnomAD CSV for the protein and the query FASTA, and writes frequency modified scores. The README's paths start with ../data/, so the command is meant to be run from a folder one level below the repository root; from the root itself, replace ../data/ with data/.

quotes.text: prescott -e ../data/MLH1_normPred_evolCombi.txt -g ../data/gnomAD_v4.1.0_MLH1_HUMAN_ENSG00000076242.csv -s ../data/MLH1.fasta
The most important output is prescott-scores.txt file, which produces frequecy modified scores for the mutations.

notes: The record cited the medRxiv preprint. A published journal version exists and was used instead: Tekpinar et al., Genome Biology 26:113 (2025), PMC12054230, open access under CC BY, which the preprint's title now differs from slightly (epistatic, and structural). bioRxiv and medRxiv were not contacted today. The source repository is on the LCQB GitLab at Sorbonne, not GitHub; it was read through the GitLab API over https (plain http redirects), and the commit pinned is 46fecb557866b4f4b9b6d60617d20ff69597cc88 of the master branch. Two licence statements disagree: LICENSE.txt, the README badge and the paper all say GPLv3, while setup.py declares Special License; the structured row records GPL-3.0 and the fact names both. ESCOTT has no released weights, so weights_licence is null. The database description for this record said ESCOTT itself uses population allele frequencies; the paper puts the frequency step in PRESCOTT and says ESCOTT relies solely on sequence and structure, so the record description should be corrected.
